region.en: Kingdoms of Gandhāra (Kashmir) and Videha (Mithila), later a Himalaya hermitage (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 乾陀羅與彌提羅兩國，後居雪山隱居處（象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: Two friendly kings, the Bodhisatta of Gandhāra and the king of Videha, each renounce thirty-thousand-year thrones for the ascetic life and meet again in the Himalaya without recognizing each other. When the Videha ascetic hoards leftover salt for a saltless day, his friend rebukes him so harshly that they quarrel, exchange pointed verses on rebuke and courtesy, and are reconciled, both attaining the Brahma heaven.
summary.zh: 乾陀羅菩薩王與彌提羅王本為摯友，先後捨棄三萬年王位出家，在雪山重逢而不相識。彌提羅仙人貯鹽備無鹽之日，遭好友嚴厲呵責，二人以偈相答、終得和解，同生梵天。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living Buddhist tradition; freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: Long ago the Bodhisatta was crown prince of the Gandhāra kingdom and became king on his father's death, ruling righteously while the king of Videha reigned in Mithila; the two had never met but trusted each other as friends. In an age when people lived thirty thousand years, on a full-moon fast day the Gandhāra king, seated on a jewelled dais, saw the moon's light swallowed by the eclipse-demon Rāhu. Taking the dimmed moon as an omen, he resolved that his kingdom had become the trouble that clouded him, handed his realm to his ministers, and went to the Himalaya as an ascetic, attaining deep meditative power. The Videha king, hearing the news from merchants, thought that his friend must have seen the good of that life, gave up his three-hundred-league kingdom and its sixteen thousand dancing girls without a thought for his children, and followed him into the forest, living on wild fruit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 406 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The two ascetics met without recognizing one another and lived together in friendliness, the Videha man serving his senior. One day, as they talked of the Law under a tree while Rāhu again veiled the moon, the elder explained that the darkened moon had once driven him from his throne. The astonished younger man discovered they were old friends. Later, descending from the Himalaya for salt and vinegar, they lodged at a frontier village; one day the villagers gave much salt, and the Videha ascetic kept the remainder rolled in grass for a saltless day. When he served the hoarded salt, the Bodhisatta rebuked him in verse: a man who had flung away sixteen thousand prosperous villages was now hoarding salt. The offended man answered with verses telling his friend to practice what he preached, and the exchange of righteous but pointed stanzas nearly broke their friendship.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 406 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Bodhisatta insisted that though a hearer might take offense, righteous words leave no stain on the speaker, and compared himself to a potter who strikes a vessel again and again until it is well baked; untrained men wander blindly like a buffalo, but the disciplined walk straight. The Videha ascetic begged pardon for his peevish temper, asked to be admonished ever after, and the two returned to the Himalaya in peace. The elder taught him the way of mystic meditation; the younger mastered it, gained the higher powers, and both, never abandoning their trance, were destined for the Brahma world. The Buddha identified the birth: the Videha ascetic was Ānanda, and the king of Gandhāra was himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 406 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

region.en: Sāvatthī and Benares
region.zh: 舍衛城與波羅奈

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: Queen Mallikā rose from garland-maker's daughter to chief queen of Kosala in a single day through the merit of giving the Buddha three portions of sour gruel. The Buddha explains that of old a poor laborer gave four portions of gruel to four silent Buddhas and, remembering that gift all his life, was reborn as king of Benares who sang of his fortune at his coronation.
summary.zh: 茉莉皇后因布施佛陀三團酸粥，一日之間由花鬘師之女升為憍薩羅王后。佛陀說往昔貧僕以四團粥施四位獨覺佛，一生憶念此施，來生為波羅奈王，於灌頂大典唱其幸運。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: Mallikā, beautiful and good, daughter of the chief garland-maker of Sāvatthī, met the Buddha at sixteen on her way to the flower garden and offered him three portions of sour gruel she carried in her flower basket. The Buddha smiled and told Ānanda that by the fruit of that gift the girl would become chief queen of the king of Kosala that very day. Returning from a defeat in battle, the king heard her singing, was drawn to the garden, and finding her fearless at his horse's bridle, rested in her lap, made her mount behind him, and at evening installed her as chief queen amid great pomp. When the Brethren marveled at the power of Buddhas, the Master told how of old wise men gave gruel without salt or oil to silent Buddhas and won royal glory in their next birth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 415 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the days of king Brahmadatta in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born poor and worked for wages. One morning he bought four portions of sour gruel for his breakfast and, meeting four silent Buddhas (paccekabuddhas) on their alms round, joyfully offered them the food with spread sand, seats of leafy boughs, and the water of donation, praying that the gift make him never again poor and lead him to omniscience. The Buddhas ate and departed to the Nandamūla cave. Remembering them daily until death, he was reborn in the womb of the chief queen of Benares as prince Brahmadatta; from childhood he clearly recalled his former life, learned all the arts at Taxila, became viceroy and then king, and married the beautiful Kosala princess.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 415 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the day of his parasol festival the king surveyed his splendor from the throne—treasuries, sixteen thousand dancing girls like nymphs of heaven—and remembered that all of it had come from four portions of gruel, so his heart filled with joy and he sang two verses of triumph that spread through the palace and city. His queen longed to know the song's meaning and chose that as her boon; the king, unwilling to tell it in secret, prepared a jeweled pavilion and before ministers and multitude explained that a hired laborer's gift of gruel to four passionless Buddhas had ripened into all his state. The queen rejoiced, urged him to give alms daily before eating, and herself declared that in a former life as a handmaid she had once put rice in a monk's bowl and won her beauty; both built six alms-halls, kept the holy days, and went to heaven. The Buddha identified them as his own queen and himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 415 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: Kosambi, Ghosita Park (real site)
region.zh: 憍賞彌國瞿師羅園

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: A trivial dispute over left-over rinse water splits the Kosambi monastery into warring factions that even drag the lay supporters and the gods into the quarrel. Three times the Buddha admonishes the Brethren with the famous verses that hatred is never ended by hatred, then departs into solitude; only a boycott by the laypeople brings the factions to Sāvatthī to beg forgiveness.
summary.zh: 憍賞彌僧團因漱口水的小事分裂成兩派，連俗眾護法與天神也捲入紛爭。佛陀三次以「以恨止恨，恨終不滅；以愛止恨，愛乃恆存」的偈語勸誡，憤而出走獨居；直至俗眾聯合抵制，僧眾才往舍衛城懺悔求恕。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); Jataka moral material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: At Kosambi two Brethren shared a dwelling, one expert in the Vinaya and one in the discourses. When the scholar left rinsing water standing and the Vinaya master charged him with an offense, then retracted it as inadvertent, their pupils carried each master's words to the other's camp as slander. A quarrel flared, and the Vinaya expert formally expelled the other Brother for refusing to acknowledge guilt. Factions hardened on both sides until the lay supporters, the sisterhood, and even the tutelary deities up to the Brahma heavens were divided, and the uproar reached the abode of the sublime gods. A Brother brought the matter to the Tathāgata, who declared, "There is a schism, yea, a schism in the Brotherhood," and went to admonish both parties in turn, pointing out the misery of expelling others and of concealing sin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 428 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the Brethren went on quarreling in the refectory, the Master stood poised in the air after his meal and taught them the imperishable verses: those who hold the thought "he abused me, he struck me, he robbed me" will never lay their wrath to rest, but in those who do not hold such thoughts wrath is appeased; not hate, but love alone makes hate to cease—this is the everlasting law. He recalled to them the ancient kings of Kāsi and Kosala: when Brahmadatta had robbed and slain the disguised king Dīghāti, the prince Dīghavu had nonetheless spared his father's murderer, and the two had become close friends; if sword-bearing kings could be so forgiving, should mendicants be less? Seeing they would not cease, he went away, and after visiting his peaceful disciples at three lodgings passed the rains alone in the Pārileyyaka forest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 428 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The lay folk of Kosambi then consulted together: the quarreling Brethren had driven the Blessed One away, so they would offer them neither salutation nor alms until they mended their ways. Starved of honor and support, the factions journeyed to Sāvatthī and begged the Master's forgiveness. He declared the Truths and identified the Birth: the old king of Kāsi was the Buddha's own father Suddhodana, the mother was Mahāmāyā, and the long-suffering prince Dīghavu was the Buddha himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 428 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

region.en: Benares, royal park and palace
region.zh: 波羅奈王宮與御苑

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: The golden-skinned young brahmin Harita renounces eighty crores of wealth for the ascetic life but is lodged in the king's park, where the queen's careless beauty rekindles a passion slumbering for countless ages and he falls into misconduct. Confronted by the king, he refuses to lie even to save himself, confesses plainly, recovers his meditation, and returns to the forest, teaching that even deep attainments can fall before desire.
summary.zh: 金膚青年婆羅門訶利多捨八俱胝家財出家，住於王苑。王后無心之美觸動其蟄伏無量劫之貪念，遂犯過失。王親自質問，仙人寧死不誑，坦白認罪，重得禪定，返回雪山，示知深定亦易為欲所壞。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: A discontented Brother, smitten by a glimpse of a finely dressed woman, let his hair and nails grow and wished to leave the Order; the Master warned that sin is destructive, insipid, and leads to hell, and that even men of great attainment have fallen through it. Of old, when Brahmadatta reigned in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born a brahmin of eighty crores and, from his golden complexion, was called Harittaca, Young Goldskin. After burying his parents and reflecting that treasure outlives its makers, he gave great gifts in fear of death and went to the Himalaya as an ascetic, attaining the Faculties and Attainments in seven days.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 431 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Descending for salt and vinegar, he lodged in the royal park of Benares; the delighted king feasted him and gave him quarters there for twelve years. When the king marched to quell a frontier disturbance he entrusted the ascetic to the queen's care, and she served him with her own hands. One day, having bathed and put on a soft fine-cloth tunic, she lay by the open lattice; the ascetic, arriving through the air, saw her robe slip at her sudden rising, and the sinful feeling that had slept in his heart through countless ages rose like a snake from its box and scattered his meditation. Seizing her hand, he drew the curtain and misconducted himself, and daily thereafter did the same, until the scandal filled the city and the king's ministers wrote to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 431 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king disbelieved his ministers and even the queen's confession, and asked the ascetic himself in courteous verse. Harita resolved that there is no sure ground like truth—for those who forsake truth cannot win Buddhahood even seated under the Bo tree—and answered in verse: "In evil ways, great king, as thou hast heard, caught by the world's delusive arts, I erred." The king lamented that man's deepest wisdom cannot dispel the passions, and Harita named the four overwhelming passions—lust, hate, excess and ignorance—where knowledge finds no footing. Resolving to cut lust to the root, he entered his hut, rose into the air in a trance, taught the king to be vigilant, refused to dwell again where he had incurred censure, and returned to the Himalaya amid the king's tears, never falling from meditation again and passing to the Brahma world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 431 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: Benares, royal palace and river bank
region.zh: 波羅奈王城與河岸

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: A boy born to a brahmin carried off by a horse-faced ogress learns to track footsteps in the air; escaping his mother across the river with her parting gift of a tracking charm, he enters royal service. Hired to catch a palace thief, he follows footprints through the air to recover the treasure, then, forbidden by filial courtesy to name the thieves—king and chaplain—tells riddling parables that turn the mob on them instead.
summary.zh: 婆羅門為馬面夜叉所擄生子，其子善識足跡。母子渡河逃歸人間，母以尋蹤咒相贈。少年入王廷為傭，憑咒尋回王自竊之寶，因不敢指斥君王，以七則隱喻故事的「庇護反成禍患」暗示，終致民眾怒而誅王，擁立少年為王。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this of a seven-year-old of Sāvatthī who could follow his father's footsteps through the whole city to Jetavana, and declared that sages of old read footprints in the air. Of old, a queen who swore an oath over her infidelity was reborn a horse-faced ogress; she served the lord of the Yakkhas three years and was licensed to prey upon a forest road. There she seized a handsome brahmin, but falling in love made him her husband in her rock cave, closing the mouth with a great stone when she left, while she ate human flesh and served him dainties. The Bodhisatta was conceived and born to them; grown, he let his father out secretly, and when she found the stone moved, her love for her child kept her from punishing them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 432 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Learning that his mother's writ ran over a tract thirty leagues long and five broad, the boy waited until she was gone, put his father on his shoulder, and outran her pursuit to the boundary river, where her power failed and she stood weeping on the bank. Unanswered, she yet gave her son, from love, the priceless charm of tracking whatever was stolen up to twelve years after; then her heart broke and she fell dead, and he burned her body with funeral rites and brought his father to Benares. The king hired him at a thousand pieces a day, and when king and family priest staged a theft—groping about the palace, descending by ladder, circling a tank thrice, and dropping the jewels in the water—the boy, saluting his dead mother's memory, spoke the spell and read their footsteps, through the air where none walked, down ladder and wall to the tank, and restored every jewel as though he had laid it there himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 432 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Pressed to name the thieves, the boy would not accuse the king in words; instead he told old tales, each ending "My refuge proved my bane": the drowning dancer whose floating lute sank him though the river is all men's refuge; the potter crushed by the very clay bank he dug; the man who perished fetching goods from a burning house; the glutton killed by the food that feeds the world; the man broken by the June wind men pray for; the birds whose tree-boughs smoked and burst into flame, so the chief bird cried "Scatter, ye birds, our refuge proves our bane"; the wife thrown to the crocodiles by her son at the daughter-in-law's urging, who survived the pyre, terrified a treasure-seeker's exorcist by biting his tongue, and came home with a robber's jewel hoard that lured her own daughter-in-law to burn herself to death; and the old father turned out by the son he had prayed for.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 432 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: "So too, sire, the king is the refuge of his people; if danger comes from him, who shall avert it?" But the king only repeated, "Bring me the thief." At last, before the assembled town and country folk, the youth proclaimed in verse that water was ablaze and safety itself had turned to fear, that plundered realm might complain of king and priest—"Henceforth protect yourselves: your refuge proves your bane." Understanding that the king had dropped his own jewels and hunted a scapegoat, the people rose with sticks and clubs and beat the king and priest to death, then anointed the Bodhisatta and set him on the throne. The Buddha identified the birth: the father was Kassapa, and the boy skilled in footsteps was himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 432 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: Benares and the Himalaya (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波羅奈與雪山（象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: Sakka, fearing the fierce virtue of the ascetic Lomasakassapa, tempts the king of Benares with universal empire and deathlessness if the ascetic can be brought to a blood sacrifice. The sage refuses, then wavers when offered the princess Candavatī, escorts her to the sacrificial pit, and at the cries of the doomed beasts comes to himself in horror, renounces the sin, and flies back to the forest.
summary.zh: 帝釋憂懼仙人嚴峻苦行，誘使波羅奈王以轉輪王位與不死為餌，求仙人行殺生祭祀。仙人初拒，後為公主旃陀伐底所惑，攜之赴祭壇；聞將宰牲畜之哀鳴，猛然醒悟，痛悔前非，拒絕王位與公主，凌空飛返雪山。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); Jataka material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The Master told this to a Brother who longed for the world, saying that even men of highest fame sometimes incur infamy. Of old, prince Brahmadatta and the priest's son Kassapa were schoolfellows; when the prince came to the throne, Kassapa, caring nothing for power, went to the Himalaya and became the grim austerities-keeping ascetic nicknamed Lomasakassapa, Hairy Kassapa, living on gleanings. His fierce fire of virtue shook Sakka's throne, and the god resolved to break his austerity by a secret interview with the king. At midnight Sakka stood in the air in the blazing royal chamber and promised the king: if he brought Lomasakassapa to offer a sacrifice of slain beasts, he would become like Sakka, exempt from old age and death, sole ruler of all India.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 433 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The councillor Sayha carried the offer to the hermitage, and the ascetic refused in ringing verses: no island realm guarded by the sea shall tempt him to such cruelty; a curse on the lust of fame and gain; better to beg one's bread as a homeless waif than win a kingdom by crime. Sakka returned at midnight to prod the king, who complained that the sage would not come; so the god counseled him to send his daughter, the radiant Candavatī, with the promise of marriage. The princess was lovely as a celestial nymph, and at the mere sight of her the ascetic's meditation fell away; trembling with passion he asked whether the king would surely give her, mounted the chariot in his matted locks as he was, and went to Benares to slaughter for her sake.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 433 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the sacrificial pit the king had ranged the doomed beasts—elephants, horses, bulls. The watching crowd lamented that women's power is mightier than sun and moon and tide, for Candavatī had drawn grim Kassapa to deadly sin. When Kassapa raised his sword on the royal elephant's neck, the elephant shrieked with fear of death, and every beast and the whole people cried aloud. At those cries the ascetic came to himself, felt his matted hair and beard, and cried, "Alas, I have done a sinful deed unbecoming my character: this cruel act is the fruit of desire; the growth of lust I cut down to the root." The king urged him on with the promised princess, kingdom, and seven treasures, but Kassapa answered, "I do not want this sin upon my soul; keep thou thy realm and fair Candavatī," concentrated his mind, rose cross-legged in the air teaching the Law, bade the king destroy the sacrificial pit and grant an amnesty, and flew back to his hermitage, thenceforth cultivating the perfections to the Brahma world. Sayha of those days was Sāriputta.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 433 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

title.en: Pūtimaṃsa-Jātaka (The Jackal and the Wise She-Goat)

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: Himalaya slopes, goats' mountain cave (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 雪山山麓山羊洞（象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: The jackal Pūtimamsa and his wife have eaten a mountain cave of goats down to one wise she-goat. The jackals stage a fake funeral to lure her into their cave, but her wariness defeats the trick twice: first she flees at his telltale glance, then she promises to return with an escort of two thousand dogs that will eat the jackals if unfed—so the pair flee and never come back.
summary.zh: 豺狼腐肉與其妻吃盡山羊洞中群羊，僅餘智慧母羊。二豺假裝喪禮誘其入洞，兩計皆敗：母羊瞥見詐死者眼神露餉而逃；後又聲言將率二千隻獵犬赴宴，若犬不得食便噬豺狼，二豺倉皇遁去，不敢再返。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The Master admonished Brethren who kept no guard over their senses, warning that a Brother who feeds his mind on pleasant forms is ruined, like the jackal Pūtimamsa who fell from his true sphere. Of old, hundreds of wild goats dwelt in a mountain cave on the Himalaya slopes, and a jackal named Pūtimamsa lived near with his wife Vetālī. He killed a goat by some device, and both grew gross on goat's flesh while the flock dwindled to a single wise she-goat named Mātalamātā, whom even his cunning could not take. Taking counsel with his wife, he laid a plot: she was to make friends with the goat, then report that her husband was dead and beg her help to weep over and bury the body; when the goat came near the corpse, he would spring up and seize her by the neck.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 437 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The goat at first refused—her kinsfolk had all been eaten by that cruel husband—but repeated entreaties prevailed; yet on the way she made the she-jackal walk ahead and kept sharp watch. Hearing their footsteps, the jackal put up his head and rolled his eyes; the goat saw at once, cried, "This wicked wretch wants to take me in—he lies making pretence of death," and fled, with the verse, "Why thus does Pūtimamsa stare? Of such a friend one should beware, and far away should flee." The jackals reviled one another, the Buddha-interpolated stanza noting that those who look at the wrong moment, like Pūtimamsa, come to grief, while the wise know when to open and shut their eyes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 437 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The she-jackal tried again, reporting that her lord had recovered consciousness at the goat's very approach and lived; come and greet him with a well-filled bowl. The goat resolved not to be taken in but to deceive the deceiver: she agreed to come with a big escort of grey hounds, tan hounds, the four-eyed hound and the Jambuka spirit-form, five hundred dogs to each—two thousand in all—warning that if they found no food they would kill and eat the jackals themselves. Terror-stricken, the she-jackal begged her not to leave her house for fear robbers would strip it, and hurried away; then she and her lord fled the spot and never dared return. The Master identified the birth: he was the tree-deity who dwelt in that old forest and saw the whole affair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 437 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: Benares; ocean isles of spirits and Ussada Hell (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波羅奈；海上靈鬼諸島與塢沙陀地獄（象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: The unbelieving rich man's son Mittavindaka strikes his mother and is cast adrift at sea, where he passes through islands of blissful spirits doubling in number and at last enters the walled city of Ussada Hell, which to his eyes seems beautiful. Taking the razor-wheel of a tormented sinner for a lotus crown, he asks for it and sets it spinning on his own head; the Bodhisatta, wandering that hell as king of the gods, explains that greed for ever more is the wheel's price.
summary.zh: 不信佛法的富商子彌陀文陀迦毆母出海，被擲於海。他先後歷四、八、十六、三十二位天女之樂島，最後誤入四門鐵城——塢沙陀地獄，將罪人頭上旋轉的剃刀輪誤作蓮冠而求之，輪即落其頭。菩薩以天帝之身巡獄，為其解說貪得無厭之果報。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this at Jetavana of a disobedient Brother, warning that long ago, when he refused the bidding of wise men, a razor-wheel was given to him. In the days of Buddha Kassapa a Benares merchant worth eighty crores had a son, Mittavindaka, wicked and an unbeliever, though his parents were on the First Path. After his father's death his mother urged him to give alms, keep the holy day, and hear the Law; he scoffed, but agreed to sit in the cloister for a thousand pieces—and spent the night so sleeping that no word of the Law could reach his ear. Grown wealthy on two millions, he fitted out a ship despite his mother's pleas, and when she caught his hand to stop him, he struck her down and put to sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 439 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the seventh day the ship stood still for his sake; lots were cast three times and thrice fell to Mittavindaka, so his shipmates set him adrift on a raft, saying, "Let not many perish for the sake of one," and the vessel sped away. He came to an island where four female spirits of the dead dwelt in a crystal palace, happy seven days and in torment seven; in their company he tasted divine bliss, and when they went away to their penance he sailed on. So he passed an island of eight spirits in a silver palace, then sixteen in a jeweled hall, then thirty-two in a palace of gold, each time following them when their term of penance came.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 439 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last he saw a walled city with four gates—Ussada Hell, where beings condemned to hell endure their own deeds, though to him it seemed only beautiful, and he thought to enter and be its king. Within stood a tormented being supporting a razor-sharp wheel on his head, but to Mittavindaka it looked like a lotus bloom, the dripping blood like red sandalwood paste, the groans like sweetest song. "Give me the lotus you have carried long enough," he demanded; the sufferer, judging that his own deeds must be spent and this newcomer guilty like himself of smiting a mother, cast the wheel upon him, and it crushed into his head. He begged it back too late; the other had vanished.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 439 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: At that moment the Bodhisatta was making a round of Ussada Hell with a great following, and Mittavindaka, catching sight of him, cried out that the wheel pierced him like a pestle crushing mustard seeds, and asked what evil he had wrought. The King of the Gods answered in stanzas: a man of a hundred and twenty thousand pieces who would not lend a friend his ear; who fled across the perilous sea, visiting the four, the eight, the sixteen, the thirty-two, and lusted ever after more—"See now, the meed of utter greed upon thy head, this wheel." Who treads the broad highway of insatiable desire, their lot is this wheel to bear; it shall roll on till he die, no saviour appearing. So the divine being returned to his place and the other fell into great misery; the unruly Brother of the frame was Mittavindaka, and the king of the gods was the Master himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 439 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: Benares and a Himalaya hermitage under a gourd tree (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波羅奈與雪山瓠樹下隱居地（象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: Kanha, a black-skinned brahmin's son, gives away eighty crores and becomes a contented forest sage living under one gourd tree. Sakka's throne grows hot with his virtue, and the god, testing him with insults about his black skin, black food and black dwelling, hears the reply that sin, not skin, blackens a man, then grants boons—which the sage spends only on freedom from malice, lust, sickness for others, and harmlessness.
summary.zh: 黑膚婆羅門之子迦曇散盡八俱胝家財，於雪山一瓠樹下知足而居。其德行熱帝釋座，帝釋以譏其黑膚、黑食、黑居試之，仙人答曰「罪黑非膚黑」，帝釋歡喜，連賜六願，仙人唯求離瞋、離貪、願無病、願不害眾生，帝釋令樹常果，譽其德而歸。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The Master smiled one evening in the Banyan Park at Kapilavatthu, and told Ānanda that on this very spot a sage named Kanha once lived in rapt meditation, whose virtue shook Sakka's throne. Of old, a childless brahmin of eighty crores prayed for a son, and the Bodhisatta was born to his wife, black of color, and named Kanha-kumāra, Young Blackie. Educated at Taxila, married and inherited, he reflected over his inscribed treasure-plates that none of the dead could carry their wealth away; since his fortune was knit to the five deadly sins, he would give it all in alms. Seeing no lessening of the store after seven days of giving, he threw open every door and went out of the city amid the lamentations of the multitude to the Himalaya, where he chose a gourd tree for his dwelling and his only food, living on whatever fell within reach of his hand, without preference for ripe or rotten.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 440 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Attaining the Faculties and Attainments, he lived long in ecstasy, eating the tree's fruit, flowers, leaves, or bark as the seasons gave them, never once rising in greediness to pick fruit elsewhere. The power of his virtue made the yellow-stone throne of Sakka burn hot, and Sakka, surveying the world, saw the sage of dread austerity and resolved to have the Law proclaimed in trumpet tones, satisfy him with a boon, and make his tree bear fruit unending. Descending, he stood behind the sage and, to test whether mention of his looks would anger him, said in verse, "Behold yon man, all black of hue, that dwells on this black spot; black is the meat that he doth eat—my spirit likes him not!"
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 440 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: By divine insight Kanha knew his visitor and answered without turning: "Though black of hue, a brahmin true at heart, O Sakka, see; not by the skin, but if he sin, then black a man must be." He then explained the sins that blacken beings and praised the goodness of virtue, and Sakka, charmed, offered any boon. Knowing the god meant only to test him, the sage asked not for power or heaven but for deliverance from malice, hatred, covetousness, and lust toward his neighbor; questioned what evil he saw in each, he answered that hatred grows from a word to a blow to the swordstroke, that greed breeds fraud and savage loot, and that lust binds its fetters in the heart. Offered boon after boon, he asked only that disease never mar his peace, and last that no creature anywhere be harmed in body or mind on his account; Sakka made the tree bear perennial fruit, touched the sage's head in reverence, and returned, while the Bodhisatta passed to the Brahma world. Of that time, Anuruddha was Sakka and the Master was Kanha the Wise.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 440 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

title.en: Saṅkha-Jātaka (The Brahmin Saved by the Sea Goddess)

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: Benares (then called Molinī) and the open sea
region.zh: 波羅奈（古名末鄰提）與大海

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: The philanthropist brahmin Saṅkha, whose six almshalls give away six hundred thousand pieces a day, sails for the Gold Country to refill his store; on the burning road he gives his own shoes and sunshade to a silent Buddha. When his ship leaks and he swims seven days, the sea goddess Maṇimekhalā offers him heavenly food—which he refuses on his fast day—and for the merit of that single pair of shoes carries him home in a jeweled ship laden with treasure.
summary.zh: 大施主婆羅門海螺日施六十萬金，為續其施而浮海求寶；於炙熱沙路上以自著之鞋與陽傘布施獨覺佛。船漏沉沒，浮海七日，海神寶鬘以天膳相餉，彼持齋不受。神謂其施鞋之德乃今日之如意牛，遂現寶船送其歸鄉。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this at Sāvatthī of a lay brother who had feasted the Order seven days and offered every Brother's requisite, with a thousand-piece pair of shoes to the Buddha himself; the Master returned thanks, saying that of old one pair of shoes given to a silent Buddha became a refuge on the sea where refuge there was none. In those days Benares was named Molinī, and the brahmin Saṅkha, rich and devout, built almshalls at the four gates, in the city's midst, and at his own door, giving six hundred thousand pieces daily to wayfarers and beggars. Fearing his wealth would run out, he built a ship, charged his wife to let no day pass without alms, and sailed for the Gold Country to bring back riches.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 442 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: A silent Buddha on Mount Gandhamādana saw him setting out and knew that if the man gave him shoes and sunshade, that gift would be his refuge when his vessel was wrecked. Passing through the air, the Buddha alighted on the burning sand and moved to meet him; Saṅkha, delighted at the chance to sow a seed of merit, brushed the sand, spread his robe for a seat, washed and anointed the holy feet, took the shoes from his own feet, cleaned and oiled them, set them on the Buddha's feet, and gave him shoes and sunshade together. The Buddha, to increase his faith, rose through the air and was gone, and the glad merchant went on to the harbor and put to sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 442 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the seventh day at sea the ship sprang a leak that no bailing could master; all aboard cried upon their gods, but Saṅkha, anointing his body with oil, ate powdered sugar and ghee, took one servant, pointed out the direction of home from the masthead, and dived with him more than a hundred and fifty cubits from the doomed ship, swimming seven days and keeping his fast even then, rinsing his mouth with salt water. The goddess Maṇimekhalā, Jewel-zone, charged by the four guardian kings to save the shipwrecked who keep the Refuges and virtue, had kept no outlook for seven days; on the seventh she saw the brahmin, and fearing blame if he died, brought a golden plate of divine meats and bade him eat. He refused: he was keeping fast. His servant, hearing but not seeing, thought his master raved from hunger and fear, until Saṅkha described the radiant gold-besprinkled presence offering food on a golden plate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 442 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the brahmin asked what deed of his had brought such fruit mid-ocean, the goddess answered, "A solitary on the burning way, weary and footsore, thirsty, thou didst stay, O brahmin Saṅkha, for a gift of shoon: that gift thy Cow of Plenty is this day." He asked only a well-built ship to bear him home; she made one of the seven precious things, eight hundred cubits long, with sapphire masts, golden cordage and silver sails, filled it with treasure, and set both brahmin and servant aboard, bringing them to Molinī, where the wealth was stored in his house. All his life he gave without end and kept virtue, and at his death he and his man went to swell the hosts of heaven. Of that time, Uppalavaṇṇā was the goddess, Ānanda the servant, and the Master the brahmin Saṅkha.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 442 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

title.en: Takkāriya-Jātaka (The Wise Boy and the Pit)

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: A village of Kasi and the cemetery road
region.zh: 迦尸某村與墓地道上

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: A dutiful son supports his aged father despite a shrewish wife who provokes quarrels; she finally tricks him into planning the old man's murder at a cemetery. Their seven-year-old son, who has overheard the plot, digs a second pit beside the first and tells his father he will bury him there in his turn, exactly as family custom goes—until the father repents, expels the wife, and later takes her back tamed by the boy's staged test.
summary.zh: 孝子奉養老父，妻屢挑撥，終設計誘其於墓地坑殺父親。七歲稚子偷聽陰謀，同赴墓地，在旁另掘一坑，說將來亦依「家傳規矩」如此葬父。父大驚悔悟，逐妻出門；後妻聞子偽稱父再娶，懼而求恕，馴順持家，一家和樂生天。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The Master told this of a layman who rose early to prepare tooth-twigs and gruel for his old father and so supported him, though his wife, a low creature, first served the old man well and then began to plague him—water too hot or too cold, food oversalted or raw—and to cry, "Either your father leaves this house, or I!" The husband refused; frightened, she craved pardon and behaved again, but the Master recalled that in a former life this man had obeyed her, and only a wise child stopped the parricide. Of old, in a village of Kāsi, lived Vasitthaka, who supported his parents and, after his mother's death, his father.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 446 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: This time the wife's dinning prevailed: the decrepit old man was sure to die soon, she said; take him at daybreak on the plea of collecting a debt, drive him to the cemetery, throw him in a pit, break his head with the spade, cover him with earth, and come home crying that you were robbed. Vasitthaka agreed and made ready the cart—but his wise seven-year-old son had overheard everything, and resolved to prevent the murder. He ran ahead and lay down beside his grandsire, and when the cart set out he climbed in with them, so that father, son and boy all came to the cemetery, where Vasitthaka, hidden from them, began to dig a pit with spade and basket.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 446 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy followed and, as though innocent, asked why his father dug in Death's acre where no bulbs or herbs grew. "Thy grandsire is very weak and old, oppressed by manifold ailments; him will I bury in a pit to-day." "Thou hast done sinfully in wishing this, and for the deed, a cruel deed it is." Then the child caught up the spade and dug a second pit hard by, and to his father's question answered in verse, "I too, when thou art aged, father mine, will treat my father as thou treatest thine; following the custom of the family, deep in a pit I too will bury thee." The father cried out against the harsh saying, but the boy answered that sin against father or mother leads surely to hell, while feeding them leads to heaven, and that he was no ingrate—the sin once done could never be undone, and the ill-conditioned wife must be expelled lest she work more woe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 446 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Vasitthaka, well pleased, drove home with son and father, thrashed the exulting wife, and bundled her out of doors. Then, at the boy's counsel, he staged a day's errand to fetch a supposed niece to tend the household; the neighbor women told his wife her husband had gone for another mate, and she fled to her son's feet crying that she had no other refuge and would tend the old man like a beauteous shrine. The boy bade his father take her back as one tames an elephant, and she, reconciled, was thenceforth righteous and watched over husband, father-in-law, and son; the two men followed the boy's advice, gave alms, and went to heaven. The Master identified them all as the same family of the present, and the wise boy as himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 446 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: Kosambi and a bamboo grove
region.zh: 憍賞彌與竹林

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: A falcon has eaten a forest flock of fowls down to their wise chief, who lives cautiously in a bamboo thicket. Three times the falcon courts him with offers of friendship and shared feeding; three times the fowl refuses, and in a thundering discourse on the kinds of men not to be trusted—liars, the self-interested, the smooth-spoken—makes the woods resound until the falcon gives him up.
summary.zh: 鷹鳥吃盡林中雞群，僅餘謹慎的雞王，匿於竹林。鷹三度示好，願為友共食；雞王三拒，並誦偈宣說不可信任之人——誑語者、自私者、巧言令色者——聲震林野，諸天喝采，鷹知難而退。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: In the Bamboo Grove the Brethren discussed the wickedness of Devadatta, who was suborning archers to murder the Master; the Buddha told them it was not the first time. Of old, in Kosambi reigned a king named Kosambaka, and the Bodhisatta, hatched from a wild hen in a bamboo grove, grew to be chief of several hundred forest fowls. Not far off lived a Falcon who caught and ate the fowls one by one until the Bodhisatta alone was left; but he took such care in seeking food and dwelt so deep in the bamboo thicket that the falcon could not reach him, and set himself to think out a trick instead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 448 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Alighting on a branch hard by, the falcon called out that the fowl need not fear him—he only wished to make friends, and named a place where food was plentiful, proposing they feed together and live in company. "Betwixt you and me no friendship can ever be; begone!" was the answer. Pleading his former sins and promising never again, he was refused a second time; a third refusal followed: with a creature of such qualities there must never be friendship. And the fowl made the wide woods resound, the deities applauding, with his seven-stanza discourse: trust not in those whose words are lies, nor the self-interested, nor sinners, nor the too-pious; some men are like cattle, thirsting and greedy, with soothing words but no deeds; they hold out dry hands while the voice conceals the heart; put no trust in fickle man or woman, in the pact-breaker, in the man of evil ways like a keen sword in its sheath, in smooth flatterers—for when the evil-minded sees food or gain, he will work all ill and first will be your bane.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 448 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Four stanzas followed from the King of the Faith, words inspired by a Buddha's insight: many a foe follows in friendly show, as the Fowl left the Falcon so bad men should be left; who is slow to read events falls under his foes' control and repents too late; who reads them quickly flies his foes as the Fowl the Falcon's toils; and from such deadly, deep-set snares the man of seeing eye should fare afar. Then the fowl reproached the falcon to his face—"If you continue to live in this place, I shall know what to do"—and the falcon flew away to another place. The Master identified the birth: the falcon was Devadatta, and the Fowl was himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 448 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

title.en: Cakkavāka-Jātaka (The Crow and the Ruddy Geese)

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: Benares and the Ganges bank
region.zh: 波羅奈與恆河岸

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: A greedy crow, sated with Benares carrion, flies to the Ganges in hope of finer fare and finer color, and questions a beautiful ruddy goose on what he eats. The goose explains that he feeds harmlessly on weeds while the crow's blackness comes from sin, fear and a diet of wrong; the crow will none of the lesson, caws, and returns to the dunghill.
summary.zh: 貪心烏鴉厭棄波羅奈腐屍，飛至恆河欲得美色美食，向一對赤雁問食。赤雁答以己食水草無害，鴉之黑色源於罪業、恐懼與不義之食，勸其捨惡行善；鴉不納諫，呱呱而返糞堆。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The Master told this of a greedy Brother who, dissatisfied with his mendicant garb, marched about asking where the next meal for the Order might be, and showed great delight at any mention of meat. "Brother," said the Master, "long ago by reason of greed you were not satisfied with the dead bodies of elephants and other offal in Benares, and went away into the mighty forest." Of old, when Brahmadatta was king of Benares, a greedy Crow, not content with the elephant corpses and all the other offal of the city, wondered what the forests might hold and flew off; but neither did the wild fruits content him, and he made his way along the bank of the Ganges.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 451 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: There he spied a pair of Ruddy Geese, very beautiful, and thought that on such a river bank they must find plenty to eat—if he could eat their food, doubtless his own color would grow fine like theirs. So he perched near and asked them in verse: fine-colored, fair of form, all plump and red of hue, sitting on the Ganges' bank feeding on pike and bream and carp and all the fish that swim the stream. The Red Goose contradicted him: "No bodies from the tide I eat, nor lying in the wood; all kinds of weed—on them I feed; that, friend, is all my food." The crow said he could not credit it—he lived on village food soused with salt and oil, a mess of clean rice poured on his meat, yet his color was not like the goose's.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 451 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the Ruddy Goose declared the reason of his ugly color and the way of righteousness: "Beholding sin your heart within, destroying humankind, in fear and fright your food you eat; therefore this hue you find. Crow, you have erred in all the world by sins of former lives; you have no pleasure in your food; 'tis this your color gives. But, friend, I eat and do no hurt, not anxious, at my ease, having no trouble, fearing nought from any enemies. Thus you should do, and mighty grow, renounce your evil ways; walk in the world and do no hurt; then all will love and praise." "Don't prate to me of your manner of feeding!" cried the crow, and cawing "Caw! Caw!" flew away through the air to the dunghill of Benares. The greedy Brother was established in the Third Path at the lesson's end; the goose's mate was Rāhula's mother, and the Ruddy Goose was the Master himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 451 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: City of Asitāñjana in the Kamsa country and the flying city of Dvāravatī (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 荅沙國阿悉多雅典那城與飛城多味那（象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: This Jataka is the Buddhist version of the Krishna legend: princess Devagabbhā, doomed by prophecy to bear the destroyer of the Kamsa line, secretly swaps her ten newborn sons for the servant Nandagopā's daughters; the Ten Brothers grow into conquerors, take the flying city of Dvāravatī by pinning it with iron chains, and divide all India. Later the wise Ghaṭapandita cures his brother Vasudeva's grief for a dead son by feigning madness and demanding the hare in the moon, and the clan is at last destroyed, as foretold, by clubs sprung from an acacia knot.
summary.zh: 此本生為佛教版黑天傳說：公主天護女因預言其子將滅荅沙族而幽於塔樓，私下以乳母十女換十子。十勇士長成為王，以鐵鏈釘住會飛的多味那城，征服全印度。後瓶賢以佯瘋索月兔之智療兄喪子之慟；全族終因相思木結之棒自相殘殺而滅亡，正如預言。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka that parallels the Hindu Krishna narrative (Vasudeva, Balarama, Kamsa); retold freely as canonical Buddhist scripture of a living tradition; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The Master told this to a lay brother who grieved immoderately for a dead son, recalling the Mad-Kundali Birth. Of old, king Mahākamsa reigned in Asitāñjana in the Kamsa country with sons Kamsa and Upakamsa and one daughter, Devagabbhā, of whom the soothsayers foretold that a son of hers would destroy the country and the lineage of Kamsa. Too fond to kill her, the brothers shut her in a round tower to live unwedded and watched. But Upasagara, an exiled prince of Madhurā, climbed by night to the tower with the help of Nandagopā, the serving-woman whose husband guarded it, and Devagabbhā conceived; spared because she first bore a daughter, she was married to Upasagara and settled in the village of Govaddhamāna. Thenceforth, whenever she bore a son, she secretly swapped him for a daughter Nandagopā bore the same day—ten sons for ten daughters—and no soul knew the secret.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 454 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The ten sons, known as the Ten Slave-Brethren, were Vasudeva, Baladeva, Candadeva, Suriyadeva, Aggideva, Varunadeva, Ajjuna, Pajjuna, Ghatapandita and Aṅkura. Fierce and strong, they took to plundering until even the king's tribute was robbed, and their supposed father, in fear of his life, confessed they were Upasagara's sons. The king set a trap: a grand wrestling match, with the champions Cānura and Muṭṭhika to hold and kill them. But Baladeva whirled Cānura round his head by an elephant-girth and dashed him dead, and crushed out Muṭṭhika's eyes and killed him too; dying, Muṭṭhika prayed to become a goblin that might devour his slayer, and became one in the forest of Kāḷamattiya. Then Vasudeva threw his wheel and lopped off the king's head and his brother's, the crowd fell at their feet, and the Ten Brethren, having slain their uncles, seized the city and set out to conquer all India.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 454 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: They took Ayodhyā and imprisoned king Kālasena, but Dvāravatī, ringed by sea and mountains and goblin-haunted, escaped them: at a goblin's ass-bray the whole city rose into the air and settled on an island in the sea until the foe was gone. Consulted, the ascetic Kanhadīpanāya taught them the remedy—clasp the ass's feet, and fix great iron posts at the four gates with chains fastened to iron ploughs, so the city cannot rise. They begged the ass not to bray; it could not help braying, but the chains held the city down, the Ten entered and killed the king, and thus they conquered all India, slaying the kings of three-and-sixty thousand cities with the wheel and dividing the realm into ten shares—eleven, when Aṅkura gave his to their forgotten sister Añjanā and took to trade. Their parents died in time, for men then lived twenty thousand years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 454 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ghatapandita feigned madness, running through Dvaravati crying, "Give me a hare!"—no hare of earth, but the hare in the moon, without which, he said, he would die. "You know that praying for the impossible kills a man," he told the grieving king Vasudeva; "why then do you mourn your dead son?" No charm, root, herb or gold can bring back the ghost—you are mourning for what does not exist—and the king's grief melted like a fire quenched with water, the dart drawn from his heart. Later the princes tested Kanhadipanaya with a man rigged as pregnant; the sage foretold that in seven days he would bring forth a knot of acacia wood that would destroy the line of Vasudeva, and was killed for the saying. The knot appeared, was burned and thrown into the river, but from its ashes sprang an eraka plant; bathing there, the princes plucked its leaves, which turned to acacia clubs in their hands, and they beat one another to death. Four fled by chariot, but in the forest the goblin Mutthika swallowed Baladeva, and the huntsman Jara, Old Age, speared Vasudeva's foot, and he died—so, saving only their sister Anjana, they perished every one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 454 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

title.en: Mati-posaka-Jātaka (The Elephant Who Fed His Mother)

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: Mount Candorana and Benares (symbolic pin for the mountain)
region.zh: 旃陀羅山與波羅奈（山為象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: The magnificent white elephant-king, whose herd of eighty thousand eats the sweet fruit meant for his blind mother, leaves the herd by night to cherish her alone by a mountain lake. Rescuing a lost forester, he is betrayed by him to the king's men; captured, he will not eat a morsel without his mother, and the king, learning her plight, sets him free and founds the yearly Elephant Festival.
summary.zh: 白象王率八萬象眾，卻讓母象餓著而群象盡食甘果；遂夜半攜盲母遁居山中湖畔。救一迷途獵人反遭出賣被擒；被囚拒食，言「無母不食」。王聞其孝，釋之歸山，並建城供養，遂有每年象祭。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this of an Elder who supported his mother, praising wise men who, even born of animals, refused food for seven days when parted from their mothers. Of old, when Brahmadatta reigned in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born a magnificent all-white elephant in the Himalaya, chief of eighty thousand elephants, but his mother was blind. He sent the herd to bring her sweet wild fruit, yet they ate all of it themselves; learning this, he said, "I will leave the herd and cherish my mother," and in the night, unknown to the others, led her to a hill cave by a lake on Mount Candorana and tended her there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 455 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: A forester from Benares lost his way and lamented loudly; the elephant pitied him, drew near, and carried the man out of the forest on his back. The wicked man marked the trees and hills as he went, and when the king's state elephant had died and drumbeat proclaimed a reward for the sighting of a mount fit for a king, he led the king's trainers to the lake. The Bodhisatta knew the danger came from that man, yet resolved not to mar his virtue with anger even under knives; bowing his head, he stood immovable while the forester seized his trunk and led him seven days to Benares. There he was housed in a stable decked with garlands, and fine food was set before him—but not a bit would he eat: "Without my mother, I will eat nothing."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 455 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Asked why, he answered in verse that his poor blind mother beat with her foot on some tree-root at Candorana for lack of him. The king gave him freedom in a royal stanza—"This mighty elephant, who feeds his mother, let go free"—and the Bodhisatta drew water from the pool and sprinkled his mother, who thought the rain had come unseasonably till he bade her rise, for Vedeha, the glorious king of Kāsi, had sent him safely home. The king built a town near the lake and served the elephant and his mother continually; when the mother died and her obsequies were performed, five hundred sages came to dwell at the monastery he founded there, the king made a stone image of the Bodhisatta and paid it great honor, and to this day the folk of all India gather yearly for the Elephant Festival. Of that time, Ānanda was the king, Mahāmāyā the she-elephant, and the Master the elephant that fed his mother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 455 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: Villages of Kasi and the city of Benares
region.zh: 迦尸諸村與波羅奈城

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: Five householders of Kasi each stumble into one small sin—a stolen draught of a friend's water, a covetous glance at another's wife, a lie told to robbers, a permitted slaughter-feast, a permitted drinking festival—and each, seized with remorse on self-examination, develops insight on the spot and becomes a Silent Buddha. Standing at the king's gate they declare their sins in verse, and the king, sickened by desire, renounces his throne.
summary.zh: 迦尸五位居士各犯一微罪——偷飲友人之水、貪視他妻、對盜賊說謊、准許殺生祭、准許飲酒節——各自省察生慚，當下修得神通，成為獨覺佛。五人於王門以偈自陳罪由，王聞之厭離諸欲，捨王位出家。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The Master assembled Brethren who at midnight indulged in thoughts of sin, and told them there is no such thing as a petty sin—wise men of old, before the Buddha came, subdued their sins and attained the knowledge of a Silent Buddha. Of old in a village of Kāsi two friends went afield with drinking vessels, and one, thirsty, husbanded his own water and drank from his friend's pot. At evening, examining his day, he remembered the stolen draught and cried, "If this thirst grows upon me it will bring me to some evil birth; I will subdue my sin." Making that stolen water the subject of his meditation, he gradually acquired supernatural insight and attained the knowledge of a Silent Buddha, while his astonished friend watched the marks of a layman vanish, yellow robes wrap about him, and the figure rise poised in mid-air.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 459 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: In like manner a land-owner who looked with desire on another man's beautiful wife thought, "This desire, if it increases, will cast me into some evil birth," developed supernatural insight, attained the knowledge of a Silent Buddha, and flew to the Nandamūla cave. A father and son journeying together had agreed to deny each other to the robbers posted at the forest edge—a premeditated lie—and the son, resting after the escape, remembered the lie, repented, and became a Silent Buddha before his father's eyes. A zemindar who had laid an interdict on slaughter yet told the crowd at the spirits'-offering to slay deer and swine as aforetime saw the heaps of fish and flesh and thought, "All these creatures have been slain because of my word alone," and even for that trifle felt remorse till insight arose; and another zemindar who permitted the time-honoured drinking festival, and saw legs broken and crowns cracked in the brawls, thought, "If I had not permitted this, they would not have suffered this misery," and he too won Pacceka-Buddhahood. Five Silent Buddhas thus gathered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 459 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Some time after, the five Silent Buddhas alighted at the gate of Benares seeking alms; the delighted king invited them into his palace, served them, and asked what cause had moved men of their age to leave the world. Each answered in verse: "The water-draught of my own friend, although a friend, I stole: loathing the sin which I had done, I afterwards was fain to leave the world, an eremite, lest I should sin again"—so the first; the second the lustful glance, the third the lie to the thieves, the fourth the slaughter-feast, the fifth the drinking-bout, each with the same refrain. The king bestowed robes and medicines and let them go; ever after he loathed the pleasures of sense, would not speak to women, sat staring at a white wall till he fell into a trance, and recited his loathing of desire in verse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 459 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: His chief queen, hearing him through the door, praised the joy of sweet desire in answer, but the king replied that desire is worse than whetted swords, knives driven in the heart, a pit of live coals, or poison. Gathering his courtiers, he rose into the air before their wailing multitude, delivered a discourse, went along the path of the wind to the furthest Himalaya, and in a delightsome spot built a hermitage, where he lived the sage's life until, at the end of his days, he was destined for the world of Brahma. Of that time the queen was Rahula's mother and the Master was the king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 459 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: Ramma city (the Benares of this birth) and the Himalaya
region.zh: 藍摩城（此世之波羅奈）與雪山

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: The viceroy Yuvañjaya, riding to the park, sees dewdrops strung like pearls on every grass blade at dawn and gone by evening, and knows that the life of beings is fashioned like dew on the grass. Over his parents' pleading he renounces the throne of Benares, and his youngest brother follows him to the Himalaya hermitage; the Master tells this to show that the Great Renunciation was not made once only.
summary.zh: 儲君優闍那晨遊御苑，見露珠如珠串綴滿草尖，日昇即消，遂悟眾生之命如草上露。不顧父母泣勸，捨波羅奈王位出家，幼弟亦隨之入雪山；佛陀以此示其出家非止一世。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Brethren in the Hall of Truth praised the Buddha's Great Renunciation—how a delicately nurtured kshatriya, who might have been a universal monarch with a thousand sons, perceived the bane of desires at midnight and rode away on Kanthaka. "This is not the first time," said the Master, "that the Tathāgata has made the Great Renunciation." Of old a king named Sabbadatta reigned in Ramma city with a thousand sons, and to his eldest, Yuvañjaya, he gave the viceroyalty. Early one morning the prince drove in splendor to the park and saw dewdrops hanging like strings of pearls on tree-tops, grass-tips, branch-ends and spiders' webs. "What is this, friend charioteer?" "Dew, my lord, that falls in the cold weather." In the evening, returning, he could not see one of them, and the charioteer told him they melted as the sun rose higher.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 460 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The prince was distressed: "The life of us living beings is fashioned like dew-drops on the grass. I must be rid of the oppression of disease, old age and death; I must take leave of my parents and renounce the world." So because of the dewdrops he saw the three modes of existence as a blazing fire, and asked his father's leave in the Hall of Judgement. The king offered him anything rather than the homeless life; the prince answered that nothing was lacking to him, but he sought a refuge where old age makes no attack, and warned that if he lingered he might become a prey to age intoxicated with lusts. His mother, told the news, came swiftly in her golden litter and begged him to stay; he answered, "Like as the dew upon the grass, when the sun rises hot, so is the life of mortal men: O mother, stay me not!" And the king, unable to refuse, gave his consent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 460 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: His youngest brother Yudhiṭṭhila greeted his father and asked leave to follow the religious life, and the king consented to both. The queen wept that Ramma would be empty—the eldest of a thousand sons, like gold to look upon, has left the world the yellow robe to don—and cried "Make haste, and bless thee!" to the departing prince. The Bodhisatta first bade his parents farewell, then took his brother and went out of the city, sending back the great multitude, and the two built a hermitage in a delightsome spot of the Himalaya. There they embraced the holy sage's life, cultivated the transcendent rapture of meditation, lived on the fruits and roots of the forest all their lives long, and were destined for the world of Brahma. Of that time the father and mother were of the present king's family, Ānanda was Yudhiṭṭhila, and the Master was Yuvañjaya himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 460 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: Benares and a Himalaya hermitage (symbolic pin for the forest)
region.zh: 波羅奈與雪山隱居處（森林為象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: The Buddhist Ramayana: king Daśaratha's second queen demands the throne for her son Bharata, so Rāma-paṇḍita, his brother Lakkhaṇa and their sister Sītā withdraw to the forest until the king's death. When Bharata comes to bring them home, Rāma neither weeps nor wails, and teaches his kinsmen the doctrine of impermanence; for three years his straw slippers rule Benares from the throne, clapping together whenever a judgment is unjust, before Rāma returns to reign sixteen thousand years.
summary.zh: 佛教版羅摩衍那：十車王后妃為其子婆羅多求王位，羅摩賢者與弟吉祥、妹悉多遁入林中。父王死後，婆羅多往迎，羅摩不哭不慟，為親屬說無常法；三年間其草鞋代掌國政，判案不公則鞋自相擊；後羅摩還都，治世一萬六千年。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Buddhist Jataka sharing characters with the Hindu Ramayana (Dasaratha, Rama, Sita, Bharata)—though here Sita is Rama's sister, not his wife; retold freely as living-tradition scripture; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this to a landowner crushed by sorrow for his dead father: wise men of old who knew the eight worldly conditions felt no grief even at a father's death. Of old a great king, Dasaratha, reigned righteously in Benares; by his eldest queen he had two sons and a daughter—Rama-pandita, Rama the Wise, Prince Lakkhana, and the Lady Sita. When the queen died the king set another in her place, and she bore a son, Bharata. When the boy was seven the queen claimed the promised boon and demanded the kingdom for her son; the king snapped his fingers at her—his other two sons shone like blazing fires. Fearing she might use forged letters or bribes to have his sons murdered, he summoned them: go to a neighbouring kingdom or the woodland, and when my body is burnt return and inherit the kingdom. The soothsayers gave him twelve years more, and the sons promised to return at the twelfth year; the Lady Sita said she too would go with her brothers, and the three departed to a hermitage in the Himalaya, where the younger two gathered wild fruit and fed Rama-pandita as a father.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 461 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: King Daśaratha pined after his sons and died in the ninth year; when his obsequies were done the queen ordered the umbrella raised over Bharata, but the courtiers refused—"the lords of the umbrella are dwelling in the forest." So Bharata took the five emblems of royalty and a complete army to fetch Rāma-paṇḍita back, and coming to the hermitage found him seated at the door, unmoved, like a figure of fine gold. Bharata told all that had happened, fell at his feet with his courtiers, and burst into weeping; but Rāma neither sorrowed nor wept, and no emotion stirred in him. When Lakkhaṇa and Sītā returned with wild fruit, the wise brother considered that the young ones' hearts might break at a sudden blow, and made them stand in the pond before telling them, stanza by stanza, that King Daśaratha's life was at an end. They fainted thrice and were carried out of the water, and all sat weeping together—yet Rāma did not grieve.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 461 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Asked by what power he grieved not, Rāma-paṇḍita explained in verse the impermanence of things: when man can never keep a thing, though loudly he may cry, why should a wise intelligence torment itself thereby? Young and old, fool and sage, rich and poor—one end is sure: each man among them dies. As the ripened fruit fears its fall, so mortals fear death; the fool grows thin and pale with weeping and cannot bring the dead to life; as a blazing house is put out with water, the wise scatter their grief like cotton before the wind. One mortal dies, and straightway ties of kindred are born to another; the strong man, skilled in the sacred text and keen in contemplating this world and the next, is not vexed by any grief, however great. Hearing this discourse the company lost all their grief, and Bharata begged Rāma to take the kingdom of Benares; but Rāma would keep his father's command, and for the three years remaining he gave his brother his straw slippers: "These shall do it."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 461 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: For three years the slippers ruled the kingdom; the courtiers placed them on the royal throne when they judged a cause, and if the cause were decided wrongly the slippers beat upon each other—at that sign the case was examined again; when the decision was right, the slippers lay quiet. When the three years were over Rāma came out of the forest, and his brothers, making Sītā the queen consort, performed the ceremonial sprinkling and gave him the kingdom. Standing in a magnificent chariot he entered Benares in solemn procession, mounted the great terrace of his splendid palace Sucandaka, and reigned there in righteousness sixteen thousand years, then went to swell the hosts of heaven. The Master identified the Birth: king Suddhodana was Daśaratha, Mahāmāyā the mother, Rāhula's mother was Sītā, Ānanda was Bharata, and he himself was Rāma-paṇḍita.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 461 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: Seaport of Bharukaccha and the marvellous far seas
region.zh: 婆留醯遮查海港與諸奇海

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: Suppāraka, blind from salt water yet master of all seamanship, leads seven hundred merchants through a chain of marvel seas, netting diamonds, gold, silver, emeralds and coral while hiding their names to curb their greed. Driven toward the VALābhāmukha sea whence no ship returns, he performs an Act of Truth—he has never knowingly taken a life—and the ship flies home in a single day, leaping over eleven hundred cubits to the mariner's door.
summary.zh: 善導尊者雖盲於海鹽，而盡通航海之術，率七百商人歷諸奇海，以漁網暗取金銀珠寶珊瑚而不言其名以抑貪心。船入無回路之婆羅菟海，乃以真實語誓願救船——誓畢，船一日還鄉，躍過一千一百肘而至其門。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Brethren praised the Buddha's matchless wisdom, and the Master said that even when his knowledge was immature he was wise—blind though he was, he knew by the signs of the ocean what jewels lay hidden there. Of old a king named Bharu reigned over the seaport of Bharukaccha, and the Bodhisatta was born to the family of a master mariner there, amiable and golden-brown; by sixteen he had mastered the whole art of seamanship, and with him aboard no ship ever came to harm. In time the salt water destroyed both his eyes, so he entered the king's service as valuer of elephants, horses, pearls and gems. Feeling all over a state elephant, he named it deformed behind from a fall at birth; a state horse lacking its dam's milk; a chariot made of a hollow tree; a royal rug with a rat-hole—each judgment proved true, yet the king paid him only eight pieces a time, and Suppāraka, judging his king a barber's brat, went home to the seaport.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 463 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Merchants fitting out a ship could find no skipper better than the blind wise man, and pressed him till he consented. For seven days all went well; then an unseasonable wind carried the vessel four months over a primeval ocean until she reached the Khuramāla Sea, where fish with razor-like snouts dived and rose. "Merchants come from Bharukaccha, seeking riches to purvey—this is Khuramālī ocean," he answered. In that sea diamonds lie; but knowing that if he told them they would sink the ship in greed, he lowered a net as if to catch fish, hauled up a store of diamonds, cast the worthless cargo overboard, and said nothing. So they passed the Aggimāla sea blazing like a bonfire, where he netted gold; the milky Dadhimāla sea, where he netted silver; the kusa-grass-green Kusamālī sea, where he netted emeralds; and the reed-like Nalamālī sea, where he netted coral.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 463 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then they came to the Valabhamukha Sea, where the waters are sucked away and rise on every side in sheer precipices, a wave standing like a wall with a roar to burst the ear and break the heart. "Once a ship gets there she will sink and go to destruction," said the Great Being, and seven hundred souls aboard cried out like those burning in the lowest hell. "Except me no other can save them; I will save them by an Act of Truth." He had them bathe him in scented water, put new garments on him, and set a full bowl in his hands at the ship's prow, and there performed the Act of Truth: "Since I can myself remember, since intelligence first grew, not one life of living creature have I taken, that I knew—may this ship return to safety if my solemn words are true!"
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 463 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Four months they had voyaged in far regions; now, as though endued with supernatural power, the ship returned in a single day to Bharukaccha, and even crossed the dry land, leaping over a space of eleven hundred cubits to rest before the mariner's door. Supparaka divided the treasure among the merchants—"this is enough for you: voyage on the sea no more"—discoursed to them, and after a life of giving went to swell the hosts of heaven. The Master was the wise Supparaka.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 463 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: A carpenter village outside Benares and the Himalaya woods
region.zh: 波羅奈城外木匠村與雪山林地

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: A lion lying under a palāsa tree is struck by a falling branch and, blaming the tree-deity, vows to tear the tree out root and branch. Meeting a carpenter seeking wheel-wood, he helpfully recommends the palāsa; but the tree-spirit, disguised as a woodman, persuades the carpenter that a wheel rimmed with a black lion's neck-skin is strongest—so the carpenter kills the lion, fells the tree, and both destroyer and destroyed perish together.
summary.zh: 黑獅臥波羅樹下，為落枝所傷，遷怒樹神，誓將樹連根拔起。遇木匠尋製輪之木，獅獻計薦波羅木；樹神化為樵夫，教匠人以黑獅頸皮包輪緣最堅，匠人遂殺獅伐樹——相爭者同歸於盡。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this on the bank of the river Rohinī to kinsmen taken up with a family quarrel. Of old, when Brahmadatta was king of Benares, there stood without the city a village of carpenters, among them a brahmin carpenter who gained his living bringing wood from the forest and making carts. In the Himalaya region stood a great palāsa tree, at whose root a black lion used to lie when hunting. One day a wind smote the tree, a dry branch fell on the lion's shoulder, and the pained beast leapt up in fear; finding no pursuer, he decided that the tree-deity could not away with his lying there, and in unseasonable anger struck the tree, crying that in a few days he would tear it out root and branch and chop it into chipmeal, and away he went in search of a man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 475 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The brahmin carpenter had come that very neighbourhood in a waggon with two or three men to get wood for his trade, and was searching with adze and hatchet when the lion, hoping to see the back of his enemy, stood under the tree and hailed him in verse: what tree is it you want, O man with the axe? Amazed that a beast could talk like a man, the wright asked what wood made good cart-wheels, and the lion gladly answered, "Not sal, acacia, not mare's-ear, much less a shrub is good; there is a tree they call palāsa, and there's your best wheel-wood," and described its drooping branches so the man might know it, promising it would do for spoke, felloe, pole or any part of a cart. Joyful, the lion moved aside, and the wright began to fell the tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 475 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The tree-deity thought, "I never dropped anything on that beast; he fell in a rage out of season, and now he is for destroying my home, and I too shall be destroyed. I must find some way of destroying his majesty." Taking the shape of a woodman, the spirit came up and asked what the man would do with the tree; told it was for a cart-wheel on a black lion's advice, the spirit praised the plan but counseled more: flay the skin from a black lion's neck, a strip four fingers wide, and bind it round the outer edge of the wheel like a sheath of iron—then the wheel will be very strong and you will gain a great deal. "But where can I get the skin of a black lion?" "How stupid you are! Go and find the lion who told you of this tree, bring him here, and while he suspects nothing and points out where to cut, wait till he sticks out his jaw, smite him with your sharpest axe, kill him, take the skin, and fell the tree at your leisure."

passages.text: The delighted carpenter killed the lion, cut down the tree, and went his way. "Thus palasa tree contends with beast, and beast with tree contends; so each with mutual dispute to death the other sends"—and so among men, where feud or quarrel arises, men cut capers peacock-wise; learn peace with all men, said the Master, and the quarrelling kinsmen were reconciled. Of that time the Master was the deity who lived in that wood and saw the whole business.
